body.text: Women are increasingly in the rooms where decisions are made, but presence doesn’t automatically translate to influence. As the United Nations (UN) Women, Peace and Security (WPS) agenda enters its 27th year, defence and security institutions should focus on creating the conditions that can close that gap.

Last month in The Strategist, I argued that the WPS agenda had an influence problem. While security institutions have become much better at including gender and women’s perspectives, those views often remain disconnected from the places where key decisions are made.

UN Security Council Resolution 1325, the resolution that created the WPS agenda in 2000, was never intended merely to increase the number of women in peace and security institutions. It aimed to integrate gender perspectives and women’s meaningful participation in decision-making, challenge unequal power relations and transform how security is understood, prioritised and practised.

Researchers have shown how WPS commitments are absorbed into institutional practices without influencing power and decision-making structures. Building on these important critiques, my research on the incorporation of WPS commitments into the UN’s protection framework and NATO’s human security agenda shifts the focus from whether institutions have adopted WPS to how its gender commitments and women’s participation can become influential. If transformation does not automatically follow from institutional inclusion, the critical question is: under what conditions does meaningful transformation become possible?

Transformation is best understood as a progression rather than a single achievement. Institutions integrate gender commitments and participatory practices into policies and organisational arrangements. Those commitments then become visible through policies, operational guidelines, representation and engagement. But transformation only becomes possible when those commitments acquire sufficient influence to shape priorities, planning assumptions, decision-making processes and authority itself. Influence is the missing link between integration and actual institutional change.

This insight shifts attention away from counting activities and towards understanding organisational relationships. To do so, institutions need to understand what conditions enable gender commitments and participatory norms to influence authority.
Across UN and NATO data, several conditions repeatedly emerge.

The first relates to how institutions understand participation. Women’s participation becomes more influential when organisations treat it as a source of decision-relevant knowledge. Women affected by conflict often possess insights into local security dynamics, community tensions and emerging risks that external actors cannot easily access. When institutions recognise this as a form of expertise, participation begins to influence how security problems are understood rather than simply how they are determined and managed.

The second condition concerns where expertise is located. Gender advisers and specialists are often positioned alongside decision-making structures rather than within them. Influence becomes more likely when expertise is embedded in planning processes, operational assessments and leadership discussions. By extension, influence is strengthened when gender expertise is understood as a professional competency rather than specialist knowledge, and where it is distributed across institutions and actors rather than concentrated within specialist roles alone.

A third condition involves the scope of issues participation can influence. Too often, women’s participation informs engagement activities, program delivery or implementation processes while remaining disconnected from conflict analysis and strategic planning. Greater influence occurs when participatory perspectives contribute to defining problems, identifying priorities and shaping institutional understandings of security itself.

Timing also matters. Gender commitments and participation frequently enter institutional processes after key assumptions are established. At that point, they may improve implementation but are unlikely to influence strategy. Engagement becomes more consequential when it occurs early enough to shape planning assumptions before decisions are made.

Finally, accountability is critical. Most organisations can measure activity: how many consultations occurred, how many personnel received training and whether compliance requirements were met. They are much less effective at assessing whether participation changed decisions or altered institutional priorities. If influence matters, accountability systems need to evaluate the effect of participatory knowledge rather than activity alone.

Importantly, none of these conditions alone brings transformation. It emerges when they align. Together, they create opportunities for gender commitments and participation to affect organisational decision-making.

I describe this as ‘conditional transformation’. The concept recognises that transformation is neither guaranteed nor impossible. Institutions are not simply either transformative or resistant to change: an organisation may constrain gender integration or participation in some circumstances while enabling influence in others. Outcomes depend on how institutional arrangements connect commitments to gender and participation to authority.

This offers a more constructive way of thinking about the future of WPS. Debates often focus on whether implementation has succeeded or failed. Yet the experience of the past 26 years suggests that it’s more useful to assess whether institutions are creating the conditions under which participation can influence authority.

At 27, WPS remains relevant. But transformation requires more than just the presence of women, the existence of policies or the completion of activities. It should be judged by whether women and their perspectives are shaping the way security is understood and practised.
